interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through exactly how the browser decides which of two conflicting CSS rules wins.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's an ordered sequence of tiebreakers, and the browser only moves to the next one if the current one is a tie — I'd walk it in this order because that's the order the spec actually applies it in.

First, **origin and importance**: user-agent defaults lose to author styles, which lose to author `!important`, which loses to user `!important` (rare in practice, but it exists). Second, if origin/importance tie, **specificity** — a tuple of (ID count, class/attribute/pseudo-class count, element/pseudo-element count), compared left to right, where a nonzero value in an earlier position always wins regardless of the later positions. Third, if specificity also ties exactly, **source order** — whichever rule was declared later in the cascade wins.

A concrete example: `#header .nav-link` is (1,1,0); `.nav .nav-link.active` is (0,2,0). The first wins outright because 1 beats 0 in the very first position — it doesn't matter that the second selector has more classes total, because the comparison never reaches that position.

If `@layer` is involved, I'd add that it's checked *before* specificity — a rule in a later-declared layer beats an earlier layer's rule regardless of selector weight.

**Testing:** whether you know the actual ordered algorithm, or just "more specific selectors win" as a vague heuristic.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Why is reaching for !important usually a code smell, and what would you do instead?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
`!important` doesn't fix a specificity problem, it escapes the specificity system entirely — it beats every normal-importance rule no matter how weak its own selector is. The trouble is what that does to a codebase over time: the first `!important` forces a style through, and the next person who needs to override *that* has exactly one reliable tool, another `!important`, usually at a higher specificity or later in source order. I've seen real legacy CSS where a single property has three or four stacked `!important` declarations, at which point nobody can reason about which one will actually apply without testing in devtools.

Instead of adding one, I'd ask why the rule I'm fighting has specificity too high or too broad in the first place, and fix that at the source — often it's an over-specific selector like `#app .sidebar .widget .title` that should just be a single class. If the real goal is "this utility class should always win regardless of what else targets the element" — a `.hidden` visibility utility, say — `@layer` is the modern, non-escalating way to guarantee that: put the utility in the last-declared layer and it wins over anything in an earlier layer without needing `!important` at all.

The one legitimate use I keep is overriding third-party CSS I can't edit directly, where there's genuinely no other lever to pull.

**Testing:** whether you understand !important as a symptom of an upstream specificity problem, not a tool to reach for casually.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: A component library's internal CSS is beating your app's override styles even though your class looks like it should apply. How do you debug and fix that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First I'd confirm it's actually a specificity issue and not a source-order or loading-order issue — open devtools, inspect the element, go to the Computed panel, click the property in question, and read the list of competing rules it shows in resolution order. That tells me immediately whether my rule lost on specificity or simply loaded before the library's stylesheet.

Component libraries often ship internal selectors that are more specific than a naive override expects — a nested selector like `.Modal_wrapper .Modal_body button` easily out-specifies a plain `.my-button` override, even though intuitively "my class should win because I wrote it more recently." Recency only matters when specificity is already tied.

My fix, in order of preference: raise my override's specificity to match or exceed the library's (matching its nesting depth, or adding one more class), rather than reaching for `!important` immediately. If the library supports `@layer` — many modern ones do specifically for this reason — my unlayered app CSS will automatically outrank anything the library wrapped in a named layer, regardless of selector weight, which is the cleanest fix if it's available. If neither is workable, a scoped `!important` on just that one override is the last resort, not the first move.

**Testing:** whether you can diagnose this as a specificity/layering problem methodically, rather than reaching for !important on the first sign of trouble.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging

interviewQuestions.question: How would you structure CSS for a large, multi-team codebase to minimize specificity wars before they start?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat specificity discipline as an architectural decision made up front, not something to firefight later. A few concrete moves: keep every component's own selectors at a single, low, consistent specificity — one class per rule, no ID selectors in application CSS ever, no more than one level of nesting even in a preprocessor. That alone removes most accidental override fights, because two rules of equal specificity resolve predictably by source order instead of an unpredictable tuple comparison.

On top of that, `@layer` gives an explicit, declared priority order — something like `@layer reset, base, components, overrides, utilities;` — so a utility class always wins over a component style and a component style always wins over a base style, by construction, regardless of how specific any individual selector happens to be. This is strictly better than hoping teams remember to keep selectors weak, because it's enforced structurally rather than by convention.

The alternative many teams reach for is sidestepping the cascade almost entirely — CSS Modules or CSS-in-JS generate unique, flat class names per component so there's rarely a cross-component collision to resolve in the first place, and utility-first frameworks like Tailwind keep every class at the same minimal specificity by design. Which of those fits depends on the team's tooling appetite, but the underlying goal is the same: make specificity boring and predictable, not something anyone has to compute by hand during a deploy-blocking bug.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about specificity at the system-design level, not just the single-selector level.
